etymology: Hebrew Ulai, a river or canal beside Shushan (Susa) in the province of Elam, the setting of one of Daniel’s visions.
biblical_def: The Ulai is the river beside which Daniel was shown the future of empires. In the third year of Belshazzar the prophet was carried, in vision, to the eastern citadel: “I was at Shushan in the palace, which is in the province of Elam; and I saw in a vision, and I was by the river of Ulai” (Dan 8:2). There the ram and the he goat contended, Media-Persia and Greece, and there the voice of God gave the command that unlocks all prophecy: “I heard a man’s voice between the banks of Ulai, which called, and said, Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision” (Dan 8:16). The vision itself came to Daniel “after that which appeared unto me at the first” (Dan 8:1), and its weight overwhelmed him: “I was afraid, and fell upon my face: but he said unto me, Understand, O son of man: for at the time of the end shall be the vision” (Dan 8:17). The Ulai preaches that the LORD reveals the course of empires before they rise, and sends His angel to give understanding to His servants. The kingdoms of Persia and Greece marched across history as God had shown by the river, centuries in advance. Prophecy fulfilled is the seal of divine authorship. By the banks of Ulai a captive Jew was shown the end from the beginning, that the church might know her God rules the ages and keeps His word.
webster_summary: A river beside Shushan in Elam where Daniel saw the vision of the ram and the goat (Dan 8:2,16); a witness that God reveals the course of empires and sends His angel to teach His servants.

corruption_paragraphs: The Ulai stirs no modern quarrel of its own, but the vision given beside it rebuffs the unbelief that would empty prophecy of prediction. Because Daniel foretold Media-Persia and Greece with such precision, the skeptic must date the book after the events, for a Bible that truly knows the future is intolerable to a closed and godless view of history.

The historical-critical assault on Daniel — the claim that its prophecies are prophecy-after-the-fact, composed in the Maccabean age — is not a discovery but a presupposition: it begins by denying that God foretells, then dates the text to fit. The believing church receives Daniel as it stands, a sixth-century prophet shown the ages by the river of Ulai. Prophecy fulfilled is the seal of divine authorship (Isa 46:9-10). The God who named the ram and the goat before they charged is the God who keeps every promise, and by the banks of Ulai He assures His people that He rules the empires and the end.

etymology: Hebrew Shushan, “lily,” the city of Susa, a royal capital of Persia and the setting of Esther and of Nehemiah’s burden.
biblical_def: Shushan, whose name means lily, was a winter capital of the Persian kings and a great stage of God’s hidden providence. There Nehemiah served and grieved: “it came to pass in the month Chisleu, in the twentieth year, as I was in Shushan the palace” (Neh 1:1), when word came of Jerusalem’s broken walls. There the drama of Esther unfolded: “in those days, when the king Ahasuerus sat on the throne of his kingdom, which was in Shushan the palace” (Est 1:2). In Shushan Haman cast his lot to destroy the Jews, and in Shushan his gallows stood empty for himself. There Esther resolved upon her perilous errand: “Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me” (Est 4:16). And there Mordecai spoke the word that names the whole book’s secret: “who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Est 4:14). The name of God is never spoken in Esther, yet His hand governs every turn in Shushan — the sleepless night, the chosen queen, the recorded deed, the reversed decree. Shushan is the monument of providence unnamed, where the LORD preserved His people in a pagan capital without a single miracle, ordering coincidences into deliverance. The God of Shushan works unseen; the lily blooms in the hand of a hidden Gardener.
webster_summary: Susa, a royal capital of Persia and the setting of Esther and Nehemiah (Est 1:2; Neh 1:1); the great monument of God’s unnamed but sovereign providence over His people.

corruption_summary: The Persian capital of Esther and Nehemiah; the entry recovers the doctrine of providence, God ruling every turn of events unseen for His people’s good.
corruption_paragraphs: Shushan raises no modern quarrel, but the book set in it silences the notion that history is mere chance or that God is absent where His name is not invoked. In Esther the name of God never appears, yet His providence governs every reversal in Shushan — the deposed queen, the chosen Esther, the sleepless king, the reversed decree.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereign providence of God, who works no less surely when He works unseen. The secularist reads Shushan as coincidence; faith reads the same events as the fingerprints of the Almighty, who preserved His covenant people in a hostile empire without a single miracle. Mordecai’s such a time as this is the confession of every saint set in a place not of his choosing. The God of Shushan orders the smallest details into the deliverance of His own, and no lot cast against His people can prosper.

etymology: Hebrew Seveneh, the southern frontier city of Egypt (modern Aswan), used to mark the whole length of the land under judgment.
biblical_def: Syene marked the far southern boundary of Egypt, so that “from the tower of Syene” became a phrase for the utmost reach of the land. When Ezekiel prophesied against the pride of Pharaoh, he swept the whole country from north to south under the sentence of God: “I will make the land of Egypt utterly waste and desolate, from the tower of Syene even unto the border of Ethiopia” (Eze 29:10). Again the doom is total: “from the tower of Syene shall they fall in it by the sword” (Eze 30:6). The cause was Pharaoh’s blasphemous boast, the great dragon of the Nile who said, “My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself” (Eze 29:3). Egypt had made a god of its river and a god of its king, and God answered the arrogance with fire: “they shall know that I am the LORD, when I have set a fire in Egypt” (Eze 30:8). Syene teaches that no border is far enough to escape the judgment of God, and no boast of self-sufficiency stands before Him. Pharaoh claimed to have made the Nile; the LORD made Pharaoh and unmakes him. From Migdol to Syene, the whole length of the proud land lay under one word from heaven. The creature who says “my river is mine own” will learn that the earth is the LORD’s and the fulness thereof.
webster_summary: The southern frontier city of Egypt (Aswan), marking the land’s full length under judgment (Eze 29:10; 30:6); a witness that no border escapes God and no boast of self-sufficiency stands.

corruption_paragraphs: Syene fixes the far edge of a proud land brought under God’s sentence. The corruption named is Pharaoh’s blasphemy: My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself — the creed of the self-made man who credits himself with what God gave and owes thanks to none.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the creaturely dependence of man and the folly of autonomy. The modern spirit repeats Pharaoh’s boast in a thousand tongues: my life is my own, my body is my own, my river is my own, and I have made it for myself. But from the tower of Syene to the border of Ethiopia the whole proud land lay under one word of God. The Nile that Pharaoh claimed to have made was the gift of the Almighty, who set a fire in Egypt to teach the boaster that the earth is the LORD’s. Self-sufficiency is the oldest lie; Syene is its answer.

etymology: Hebrew Gichon, “bursting forth,” one of the four rivers that watered the garden of Eden, compassing the land of Cush.
biblical_def: The Gihon is the second of the four rivers of Eden, a witness to the goodness of the world as God first made it. From the garden a great water flowed and divided: “a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads” (Gen 2:10). The first was Pison, which “compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold” (Gen 2:11); “the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia” (Gen 2:13); the third Hiddekel and the fourth Euphrates (Gen 2:14). These rivers preach the original bounty of creation, a world watered and gladdened by the hand of God before sin brought thorn and curse. The Gihon, whose name means “bursting forth,” poured its fullness over lands of gold and spice, a picture of unspoiled abundance. Eden’s rivers also point forward: as a river went out of Eden to water the garden, so from the throne of God flows the pure river of water of life, and the tree of life stands on its banks in the paradise restored (Rev 22:1-2). The Gihon of the first creation is a promise of the second. What Adam forfeited, the last Adam regains; the garden lost by sin is the garden-city gained by grace, watered for ever by the river of God.
webster_summary: The second river of Eden, compassing the land of Cush (Gen 2:13); a witness to the original bounty of creation and a foretoken of the river of life in the paradise restored.

corruption_paragraphs: Gihon belongs to the true history of the garden, and its chief modern corruption is the denial that Eden ever was. The four named rivers, two of them still known by name, anchor the account in geography, not myth. Scripture presents Eden as a real place with real waters, from which flowed the bounty of an unfallen world.

The corruption to name is the mythologizing of Genesis — the treatment of Eden and its rivers as legend or symbol rather than history. But the Holy Ghost names the Gihon, the Pison, the Hiddekel, and the Euphrates as He names any river of the earth, and the New Testament rests the whole doctrine of sin and salvation on a historical Adam in a historical garden (Rom 5:12-19). To dissolve Eden into fable is to loosen the ground of the gospel. The Gihon that watered the first paradise is the pledge of the river of life that waters the last, where the curse is gone and the tree of life bears its fruit for the healing of the nations.

etymology: Hebrew Nachal Mitsrayim, “the river (wadi) of Egypt,” the seasonal watercourse marking the southwestern border of the promised land, distinct from the Nile.
biblical_def: The Brook of Egypt is not the Nile but a seasonal wadi that ran to the sea across the southern desert, appointed by God as the southwestern boundary of the land He gave to Israel. When the LORD marked out the inheritance, the line ran to it: “the border shall fetch a compass from Azmon unto the river of Egypt, and the goings out of it shall be at the sea” (Num 34:5). So too in Judah’s allotment the coast “went out unto the river of Egypt; and the goings out of that coast were at the sea: this shall be your south coast” (Jos 15:4). In Solomon’s golden day the promise was realized to its full extent: he “held a feast, and all Israel with him, a great congregation, from the entering in of Hamath unto the river of Egypt” (1Ki 8:65) — the whole breadth of the land, border to border, kept by the faithfulness of God. And the prophets set that same brook as the gathering-line of the final restoration: “the LORD shall beat off from the channel of the river unto the stream of Egypt, and ye shall be gathered one by one, O ye children of Israel” (Isa 27:12). The Brook of Egypt preaches the exactness of God’s covenant grant. He did not give a vague promise but a surveyed land with fixed borders, and He kept it to the letter in the days of Solomon, that His people might know their God performs His word to the last landmark.

corruption_summary: The wadi marking the land’s southern border; the entry recovers the exactness of God’s covenant grant, kept to the letter in Solomon’s reign.
corruption_paragraphs: The Brook of Egypt raises no modern quarrel, but its office as a fixed border rebukes the vague and sentimental reading of God’s promises. The LORD did not pledge Israel some hazy region but a surveyed land with named landmarks, from the entering in of Hamath to the river of Egypt.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the definiteness and faithfulness of God’s covenant word. What He promises He measures, and what He measures He keeps: in Solomon’s day Israel dwelt from Hamath to the brook of Egypt, the whole grant fulfilled to the last landmark. A God who keeps His promise to the exact border is a God whose spiritual promises are equally sure. The believer’s inheritance in Christ is not a mist but a measured and sealed possession, kept by the same faithfulness that ran the line to the stream of Egypt.

etymology: Hebrew Besor, “cool” or “cheerful,” a brook in the south of Judah where David divided the spoil between the strong and the faint.
biblical_def: The brook Besor is the setting of one of the noblest laws of grace in the Old Testament. Pursuing the Amalekites who had burned Ziklag, David came to it with a weary band: “David went, he and the six hundred men that were with him, and came to the brook Besor, where those that were left behind stayed” (1Sa 30:9). Two hundred could go no further: “two hundred abode behind, which were so faint that they could not go over the brook Besor” (1Sa 30:10). David and four hundred pursued, recovered all, and returned laden with spoil; and when he came again “to the two hundred men, which were so faint that they could not follow David, whom they had made also to abide at the brook Besor” (1Sa 30:21), certain wicked men would have denied the faint any share. David refused, and made it a statute in Israel: “as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff: they shall part alike” (1Sa 30:24). The brook Besor preaches the grace of the Captain of our salvation. In Christ’s army the weak and the faint are not despised nor cut off from the reward; the spoil is shared alike, for the victory is His and not the strong soldier’s. He who keeps the stuff by the brook, unable to march, yet belongs to the host and receives of the spoil. Grace, not merit, apportions the inheritance.
webster_summary: A brook in the south of Judah where David decreed the faint who kept the baggage should share the spoil alike with the fighters (1Sa 30:24); a picture of the grace that honours the weak in Christ’s host.

corruption_paragraphs: Besor rebukes the merit-reckoning that would grant reward only to the strong and the successful. The wicked men of David’s band judged the faint unworthy of the spoil because they had not fought. David overruled them, seeing that the victory was the LORD’s gift, not the achievement of the four hundred.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that in the kingdom of grace reward flows from the Captain’s bounty, not the soldier’s strength. The faint who keep the stuff by the brook, unable to march, still belong to the host and share alike. So the weakest believer, who can scarcely stand and only keeps his post, is not cut off from the inheritance won by Christ. The spoil of His victory is parted to the whole army by grace. Besor forbids both the pride of the strong and the despair of the faint: they shall part alike, for the battle and the reward are the Lord’s.

etymology: Hebrew Qedesh, “holy” or “sanctuary,” a Levitical city and city of refuge in the mountains of Naphtali in Galilee.
biblical_def: Kedesh, whose name means “holy,” was set apart as a city of refuge in the north, a sanctuary for the manslayer. When Israel appointed the refuge-cities, “they appointed Kedesh in Galilee in mount Naphtali” (Jos 20:7), and it was given to the Levites as a haven: “Kedesh in Galilee with her suburbs, to be a city of refuge for the slayer” (Jos 21:32). To Kedesh belonged Barak, whom Deborah summoned to break the northern oppressor: “she sent and called Barak the son of Abinoam out of Kedeshnaphtali” (Jdg 4:6). And when the Assyrian storm broke, Kedesh was among the first towns carried into exile: “took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor” (2Ki 15:29). The city named holy was a place of mercy: the man who had killed unawares fled there and lived, safe until the death of the high priest, when he went free. Kedesh preaches the gospel of the refuge. The manslayer running for the gate is every sinner fleeing the avenger of blood, and the city that receives him is Christ, our sanctuary and our hiding place. As the slayer was released at the death of the high priest, so the sinner is set at liberty by the death of our great High Priest, who by dying opens the gate and cancels the debt. There is refuge in the Holy One for the guilty who flee to Him.
webster_summary: A Levitical city and city of refuge in Naphtali, whose name means “holy” (Jos 20:7; 21:32); a gospel picture of Christ the sanctuary who frees the manslayer by His death as High Priest.

corruption_paragraphs: Kedesh raises no modern quarrel, but the ordinance of refuge it embodies rebukes both the cheapening and the despairing of God’s justice. The refuge did not deny that blood had been shed; it provided a lawful, God-appointed sanctuary for the one who had killed unawares, holding justice and mercy together at the gate.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gospel typified in the city of refuge. The manslayer fleeing the avenger is the sinner fleeing wrath, and the city named Holy is Christ, in whom alone the guilty are safe. As the slayer was freed at the death of the high priest, so the believer is released by the death of our great High Priest, who opens the gate by His own blood. Justice is satisfied, and mercy triumphs, not by ignoring guilt but by the death that answers it. Kedesh bids the sinner run to the refuge and live.

etymology: Hebrew Chatsor Chadattah, “New Hazor,” a town in the far south of Judah toward the border of Edom, distinct from the great Hazor of the north.
biblical_def: Hazor-hadattah means “New Hazor,” a small town in the parched southland of Judah, named once in the roll of the tribe’s uttermost cities: “And Hazor, Hadattah, and Kerioth, and Hezron, which is Hazor” (Jos 15:25). It lay among “the uttermost cities of the tribe of the children of Judah toward the coast of Edom southward” (Jos 15:21), in the dry Negeb where several towns bore the name Hazor, so that one was distinguished as New Hazor and another as Hazor which is Hezron. This is no famed Hazor of Jabin and the northern wars, but an obscure settlement of the desert frontier. The whole southern list belongs to Judah’s inheritance: “This then was the lot of the tribe of the children of Judah by their families; even to the border of Edom the wilderness of Zin southward” (Jos 15:1). Hazor-hadattah preaches, like all these forgotten border-towns, the faithful particularity of God. He did not overlook the arid edge of the land, the smallest hamlet toward Edom; He named it and gave it. The lines fell for Judah even in the wilderness of Zin, and the goodly heritage reached to the farthest, driest corner. What the world would pass over as barren and unimportant, the LORD wrote in the book of the inheritance, for He forgets none of His people’s portion, however small or however dry.
webster_summary: “New Hazor,” an obscure town in the far south of Judah toward Edom (Jos 15:25), distinct from the great northern Hazor; a witness to God’s faithful particularity to the last dry corner of the inheritance.

corruption_summary: “New Hazor” of the southern desert; the entry recovers God’s faithful particularity to the least and driest corner of His people’s inheritance.
corruption_paragraphs: Hazor-hadattah faces no modern redefinition; it is scarcely known. Yet its lone mention in the desert list rebukes the worldly measure that counts only the fertile and the famous worth recording. God named New Hazor on the arid edge toward Edom and folded it into Judah’s inheritance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the tender exactness of God’s covenant faithfulness. He did not stop His reckoning at the pleasant valleys but ran the lines to the wilderness of Zin, naming the smallest hamlet of the parched frontier. The lines fell for Judah even there, and the heritage was called goodly (Psa 16:6). So the believer’s portion in Christ reaches to every corner of his life, even the dry and barren places the world despises. God forgets no part of what He has given His own.

etymology: Hebrew Paddan Aram, “the plain (or field) of Aram,” the region of Mesopotamia about Haran, home of Laban and the patriarchal kindred.
biblical_def: Padan-aram, “the plain of Aram,” was the old country of the patriarchs, the region about Haran from which Abraham had come and to which his sons looked for their wives. Thither Isaac’s father sent for Rebekah: “Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah to wife, the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Padanaram” (Gen 25:20). Thither Jacob fled from Esau at his parents’ charge: “Arise, go to Padanaram, to the house of Bethuel thy mother’s father; and take thee a wife from thence” (Gen 28:2). In Padan-aram Jacob served twenty years, was disciplined in the school of Laban, and there God multiplied him: he “carried away all his cattle, and all his goods which he had gotten in Padanaram, for to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan” (Gen 31:18). There too his children were born: “the sons of Leah, which she bare unto Jacob in Padanaram” (Gen 46:15). Padan-aram is the place of the patriarchs’ exile and of God’s covenant faithfulness in a far land. Jacob went out with a staff and returned with two bands; the God of Bethel kept him in Padan-aram, blessed him under an unjust master, and brought him home according to the promise. The far country of Laban was the anvil on which God shaped the father of the twelve tribes. He keeps His covenant even in the land of exile, and brings His pilgrims home.
webster_summary: The region of Mesopotamia about Haran, home of Laban and the patriarchal kindred (Gen 25:20; 28:2); the place of Jacob’s exile and of God’s covenant faithfulness in a far land.

corruption_summary: The Mesopotamian home of the patriarchal kindred; the entry recovers God’s covenant faithfulness to His pilgrims in the land of exile.
corruption_paragraphs: Padan-aram raises no modern controversy, but Jacob’s long sojourn there rebukes the impatience that reads a season of hardship as God’s absence. Twenty years under a grasping master, wages changed ten times, discipline and disappointment — and through it all the God of Bethel was keeping the covenant and shaping the father of the tribes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant faithfulness of God in the far country. Jacob went out with a staff and came home with two bands, not because Laban was kind but because God was faithful. The believer’s Padan-aram — his years of exile, service, and hard providence — is the very anvil on which God forges him, and the promise that kept Jacob keeps him too. The Lord blesses His pilgrims under unjust masters and in distant lands, and in His time brings them home to the inheritance He swore to give.

etymology: Hebrew Sukkoth, “booths” or “shelters,” a town in the Jordan valley east of the river where Jacob built booths, and where Gideon rebuked the churlish.
biblical_def: Succoth, “booths,” took its name from the shelters Jacob raised there on his return from Padan-aram: “And Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built him an house, and made booths for his cattle: therefore the name of the place is called Succoth” (Gen 33:17). It lay in the valley of Jordan, a stage on the pilgrim’s road home. Long after, in the days of the judges, Succoth showed a harder face. When Gideon pursued the kings of Midian, faint yet pursuing, he asked bread of its men: “Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that follow me; for they be faint” (Jdg 8:5). But the princes of Succoth mocked him and refused, fearing to take his part before the victory was sure. Gideon returned triumphant and kept his word of chastisement: “he took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth” (Jdg 8:16). The valley of Succoth was reckoned among the LORD’s own portions: “I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth” (Psa 60:6). Succoth preaches two lessons in one place: the shelter of the pilgrim who trusts God on the road home, and the folly of the coward who withholds his bread from the LORD’s cause until he sees which way the battle turns. Faith feeds the servant of God before the victory; unbelief calculates and is chastised.
webster_summary: A town in the Jordan valley where Jacob built booths (Gen 33:17) and Gideon chastised the churlish (Jdg 8:5,16); a place of the pilgrim’s shelter and a warning against cowardly calculation in the LORD’s cause.

corruption_summary: The Jordan-valley town of Jacob’s booths and Gideon’s rebuke; the entry recovers the shelter of the trusting pilgrim and warns against cowardly calculation in God’s cause.
corruption_paragraphs: Succoth rebukes the cowardly prudence of the men who refused Gideon bread. They would not commit themselves to the LORD’s champion until the victory was certain, fearing Midian’s vengeance more than God’s displeasure. It is the eternal calculation of the fence-sitter, who waits to see which side prevails before he risks a loaf.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith feeds and supports the cause of God before the outcome is visible, while unbelief hedges and is chastised. The men of Succoth wanted the reward of the winning side without the risk of the fighting side, and Gideon taught them with thorns. The disciple is called to confess Christ and support His servants now, in the day of reproach, not to wait upon the applause of the victors. Yet the same Succoth is where Jacob built his booths and rested under God’s keeping — a reminder that the pilgrim who trusts finds shelter on the road home.
